results.title: Anthropic: AI Misuse Is Entering a New Phase: From Cybercrime to Surveillance, Propaganda and Weapons
results.author: Pierluigi Paganini
results.content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming more than a tool for people who want to do something malicious. It is increasingly becoming part of the operational machinery itself.
That is the main message emerging from Anthropic ‘s latest Threat Intelligence report, which examines malicious activity identified and disrupted between December 2025 and August 2026. The cases cover cyber operations, influence campaigns, surveillance, fraud, biological research, conventional weapons and attempts to extract the capabilities of frontier AI models.
The actors involved are equally diverse. Anthropic describes suspected state-sponsored groups, financially motivated criminals, commercial surveillance operators and politically motivated individuals. What connects many of these cases is not a new attack technique, but the way AI changes the economics, speed and scale of operations.
AI is becoming an operational layer
The report makes an important distinction from the usual discussion about AI-powered hacking.
The biggest change may not be that AI can discover a new vulnerability or write malware. It is that models can now contribute across almost the entire attack chain, from reconnaissance and tool development to exploitation, credential theft, data processing and exfiltration.
Anthropic observed operations in which AI systems executed commands against victim networks, harvested credentials and exfiltrated information. At the more autonomous end of the spectrum, multi-agent frameworks conducted reconnaissance, exploitation and data theft against several victims in parallel, sometimes for hours or days with limited human intervention.
This has an important consequence for defenders. Sophisticated attacks no longer necessarily require sophisticated attackers.
According to Anthropic, AI is reducing the gap that once separated well-funded state operations from smaller criminal groups. Reconnaissance, exploitation, coding and data analysis that previously required several specialists can increasingly be delegated to AI systems running at machine speed.
The underlying attacks are often familiar. Stolen credentials, exposed services, vulnerable edge devices, phishing and SQL injection still play a central role. What has changed is the cost of putting them together at scale.
Cybercrime becomes a production line
One of the clearest examples involves a financially motivated operation that harvested credentials from software and online services.
The attackers downloaded and analyzed 1.8 million Android application packages, searching for hardcoded secrets, while running a parallel process to collect GitHub-related credentials. The important point is not the number of apps. It is the automated pipeline connecting discovery, credential collection, validation and subsequent intrusion activity.
“One French-speaking operator going by the aliases of (MeowSHA | frkoo | blazespider) ran a distributed credential-harvesting pipeline across a fleet of 10 AWS EC2 workers. This pipeline mass-downloaded 1.8 million distinct Android APKs from multiple app-store sources, decompiled them, and scanned for hardcoded secrets with Detecting and countering misuse of AI: September 2026 12 TruffleHog.” reads the report. “Verified findings were routed in real time to a Telegram group organized into over 100 source types. A parallel GitHub organization email harvester fed a second stream of stolen GitHub Personal Access Tokens. These two credential pipelines supplied the initial-access credentials for the bulk of the confirmed breaches associated with frkoo.”
The same model appears elsewhere in the report. Attackers used AI to develop malware and phishing tools, analyze compromised environments, process stolen information and maintain access to victims.
In one campaign, stolen tokens could be replayed against Microsoft services to access mailbox contents, including deleted messages. The attackers used techniques designed to make their traffic resemble legitimate Microsoft clients. Anthropic says Claude was used to engineer and test the tooling.
This is what makes the development significant. AI does not need to invent a completely new attack for the threat level to increase. If it can automate enough of the existing process, a small team can attempt operations that previously required a much larger workforce.
Surveillance at machine speed
The report becomes even more striking when it moves beyond cybercrime.
Anthropic identified nation-state actors and commercial surveillance operators using Claude to build systems for monitoring populations, profiling individuals and analyzing social media activity. The cases involve actors linked to China, Iran and West Africa, as well as the commercial surveillance-for-hire market.
“These cases include threat actors from China, Iran, and West Africa, as well as the commercial “surveillance-for-hire” market, and range from operations carried out by a single individual to entire teams.” continues the report. “Anthropic’s Usage Policy prohibits using Claude to conduct non-consensual surveillance and profiling, and to use our services to violate individuals’ civil liberties and human rights. In every case we describe below, the threat actors violated our Usage Policy and attempted to circumvent controls designed to detect such misuse.”
In one case, a consultant working for Malian national security authorities used Claude to engineer a mass-interception platform capable of monitoring communications across the country’s mobile operators and producing dossiers on targets.
In another, Iranian actors used Claude to develop a malicious Firefox extension designed to harvest information about social-media users. Chinese operators used AI to analyze large volumes of social-media content, identify potential targets and generate intelligence reports.
One particularly revealing operation targeted Uyghur communities in Syria. An actor without Arabic-language skills used Claude to draft messages in the appropriate dialect, translate replies in real time, role-play as an expert to evaluate the operation and prepare the resulting information for a suspected human case officer.
This shows another important shift. AI is not merely analyzing surveillance data after it has been collected. It can become part of the system that decides whom to watch, how to approach them and how to turn raw information into intelligence.
Propaganda can also be industrialized
The same automation is appearing in influence operations.
Anthropic describes an operation linked with high confidence to UAE government officials in which AI supported a network of roughly 300 inauthentic social-media accounts. The operation also created a front NGO using the identity of a real organization, produced apparently independent human-rights material and ghost-wrote testimony intended for presentation to the UN Human Rights Council.
The actors also profiled 18 members of the European Parliament and journalists and prepared dossiers on UN Special Rapporteurs who had criticized UAE conduct in Sudan.
The significance is not simply that AI can generate propaganda. Political actors have been producing propaganda for centuries. The difference is that AI can make the process much cheaper and more scalable while allowing operators to generate different narratives, personas and documents for different audiences.
The line between genuine grassroots activity and centrally coordinated influence therefore becomes harder to see.
Fraud gets a human face without the human
The report also provides a remarkably concrete example of AI-powered consumer fraud.
A China-based app studio built more than 20 dating applications and used AI personas to communicate with users while advertising the services as fully human. During a two-week period, Anthropic identified more than 4,700 AI personas that interacted with at least 25,000 people.
“A China-based app studio used Claude to both build a network of over 20 dating apps and power the AI personas used to converse with users–despite advertising their service as fully human.” states Anthropic. “Over a two-week window in April 2026, we discovered more than 4,700 distinct AI personas that engaged in conversations with at least 25,000 unique individuals.”
The operation combined AI and human workers. The bots handled large volumes of conversations, while real people performed activities such as video calls and social-media interactions designed to convince victims that they were dealing with genuine users.
The reported ratio was roughly three AI personas for every real person. Claude generated around 2.36 million messages during the period examined.
This is an important preview of how AI could change online fraud. The attacker no longer needs thousands of people to maintain thousands of conversations. A small human operation can supervise a much larger artificial workforce.
The terrorism risk deserves attention
The report does not identify a confirmed terrorist attack conducted with Claude. It does, however, document activity that illustrates why AI-assisted weapons development deserves attention from counterterrorism and national-security agencies.
Anthropic identified six cases involving weapons development, procurement or intelligence gathering in China, Russia and Yemen. The cases include guided rockets, ballistic-missile simulations, anti-torpedo systems, autonomous drone swarms, electronic-warfare targeting and directed-energy weapons.
“We identified a cell of threat actors based in northern Yemen running three weapons development programs: a guided rocket that used a commodity phone-class flight computer with final-phase homing guidance; a multi-stage ballistic missile with a stated range goal above 2,000 km; and a multi-variant missile (referred to as the “R2000” set) that included a hypersonic glide vehicle variant.” continues the report.
The Yemen case is particularly significant from a terrorism perspective, even though Anthropic does not establish that the actors were a terrorist organization. A weapons-development cell used Claude Code to work on guidance, navigation and control software for a guided rocket. Multiple AI instances were assigned different roles, including coding, research and code review. The group also carried out a real-world test of a guided rocket and returned to the model afterward to analyze the failure.
That distinction matters. AI is not necessarily giving a terrorist group the ability to build an advanced weapons system from nothing. What it can do is reduce the amount of specialized engineering expertise required to modify, integrate and troubleshoot technologies that the group already possesses.
For counterterrorism agencies, this creates a potential new problem: the proliferation of technical capability may no longer depend entirely on recruiting highly specialized engineers.
Weapons development is not limited to missiles
The report provides several other examples.
One China-based actor used Claude to develop documentation and software for an anti-torpedo system, including a technical proposal of more than 200 pages and comparative analysis of US naval systems. The actor repeatedly asked the model to act as a hostile expert and criticize its own work, effectively creating an automated review process.
A Russia-based operation worked on an autonomous FPV drone swarm using Claude Code and simulation infrastructure. Other cases involved electronic warfare, air-defense suppression and intelligence gathering related to directed-energy weapons.
The pattern is consistent: AI can compress research, engineering, documentation and testing cycles.
That does not mean the model independently created these weapons. In several cases, the actors already had expertise, hardware or access to the necessary infrastructure. The AI accelerated the work around them.
Biology is an even harder problem
Biological misuse presents a different challenge because intent is much harder to establish.
Anthropic says today’s models are capable of assisting with increasingly complex scientific research, making it harder to guarantee that they cannot meaningfully support dangerous biological work.
The report describes five cases involving potentially sensitive research. They include gain-of-function work involving chikungunya, planning related to mammalian adaptation of avian influenza, an orthopoxvirus immune-evasion research proposal, optimization of venom peptides and computational redesign of toxins.
Anthropic is careful about what these cases prove. It does not claim that the researchers intended to develop biological weapons, nor that Claude enabled a biological weapon. The cases demonstrate something more subtle: dangerous research can look very similar to legitimate scientific research when viewed one request at a time.
That makes traditional content filtering much harder.
A sophisticated actor does not necessarily have to ask an AI model, “How do I build a biological weapon?” They can divide the work into apparently legitimate scientific tasks and combine the answers elsewhere.
AI is also becoming the target
Perhaps the most strategic part of the report concerns illicit distillation.
Anthropic says several Chinese AI companies attempted to extract capabilities from Claude by creating large numbers of fraudulent accounts, routing enormous numbers of queries through proxy networks and collecting model outputs for training.
Alibaba’s operation reached almost three million exchanges per day from more than 3,500 fraudulent accounts, with more than 151 million exchanges observed between May and July. The activity targeted agentic tasks, software engineering, kernel development and long-horizon reasoning.
Zhipu used hundreds of fraudulent accounts to extract and process reasoning traces. Moonshot, meanwhile, allegedly forwarded customer requests to Claude while presenting Claude’s responses as if they came from its own Kimi models.
The privacy implications are serious as well. Anthropic says some rerouted requests contained sensitive corporate information, live credentials and surveillance data. In one case, DeepSeek allegedly relayed requests containing internal AI-program specifications; another exposed credentials associated with a Russian government database.
This creates a new category of AI supply-chain risk: an organization may think it is using one AI service while its data and workloads are actually being processed by another.
The common thread is scale
The cases in the report look very different, but they point in the same direction.
AI is becoming a force multiplier for cybercriminals, intelligence services, propagandists, fraudsters, surveillance operators and potentially armed groups. It can automate the boring parts of an operation, accelerate the difficult parts and allow a small number of people to coordinate activity at a scale that would previously have required a much larger organization.
This is why the most important finding is not that AI can hack systems or generate malicious code.
The bigger issue is that AI is changing the economics of malicious activity.
A criminal group can process millions of files. A surveillance unit can turn huge volumes of social-media posts into target profiles. A propaganda operation can maintain hundreds of artificial identities. A fraud operation can hold thousands of conversations simultaneously. A weapons program can use AI to accelerate software development and technical analysis.
And in the most advanced cyber cases, AI systems can perform several of these tasks with little human intervention. Anthropic reports that humans still tend to retain the decisions that matter most, such as selecting targets and deciding how to monetize results. But the operational workload between those decisions can increasingly be delegated to machines.
That may be the real security threshold we are crossing.
The question is no longer simply whether AI can be abused. It clearly can.
The more important question is how much of a malicious operation can now be delegated to AI before a human has to step in.
Anthropic’s report suggests that the answer is already: quite a lot.
“Sophisticated and persistent threat actors continuously test our safeguards and try to circumvent the technical measures we use to detect and prevent misuse.” concludes the report. “We’ll continue to evolve our safeguards and coordinate with our partners to improve our ability to detect, disrupt, and prevent future misuse.”

Risk scores reflect objective indicators of transparency, but do not determine operators’ practices. Missing licensing data, unclear ownership, inconsistent policies, or weak documentation could indicate misconduct, but do not establish it conclusively.

Most gaming services require players to create an account using an email address or other crypto casino login credentials, and some allow access via a Web3 or wallet authentication. The authentication processes of online cryptocurrency casinos vary widely and are separate from identity verification.
Standard security protocols may include two-factor authentication, email alerts, device recognition, and withdrawal verifications. There may also be requirements for verification of identity via documents before some withdrawals are processed, depending on operator policy or regulations.
Why Search Demand Does Not Equal Player Safety
High visibility in search results or brand awareness does not guarantee quality of operation or player protection. Search ranking can be influenced by vendor marketing, affiliate visibility or player demand, not by transparent licensing, payout statistics or responsible gambling.
For that reason, this report covers operators based on evidence obtained through public records, licensing information, payment policies, and verification, rather than relying solely on popularity as indicated by search results or advertising.

“Best” is subjective in the crypto casino space. Factors players may consider include, but are not limited to, payment speed, supported cryptocurrencies, privacy, game selection, and regulation. This means that no operator is objectively better for each person, and independent reviews have begun to favor a transparent scoring system.
Rather than trying to find one single “best” operator, we will define some common metrics with which we will compare operators and the relative benefits and drawbacks.
Why Rankings Alone Are Not Enough
Rankings compress each complex evaluation into a single number without revealing the formula. Readers have no way of knowing whether the rank is based on licensing, crypto casino bonus terms, payment reliability, or commercial partnerships.
Therefore, the study compares the licensing transparency, withdrawal process, KYC, security measures, and responsible gambling measures used by the various sites, rather than the rankings.
Trust Signals and Red Flags
Important trust signals such as a visible license statement, identifiable owner, payment and verification policy, responsible gambling tools, and consistent official documentation can provide a stronger basis for independent evaluation than promotional materials.
Red flags include unverifiable licensing, anonymous ownership, vague withdrawal conditions, inconsistencies in withdrawal and other policies, claims that seem too good to be true, or marketing statements with no backing from publicly available information. The U.S. requires separate mention, as laws around the regulation of online gambling are determined at the state level, not the federal level, and as a consequence, a crypto casino may be available to players in other regions of the world, or other states of the U.S., but not in the U.S. itself or any individual state.

Why the U.S. Market Needs Separate Analysis
The U.S. online gambling market includes state-regulated online gambling, as well as offshore sites, and alternative business models such as sweepstakes casinos. Because of a patchwork regulatory environment, many characteristics of cryptocurrency markets (such as operator availability and verification, transaction taxation, consumer protections, and other regulatory characteristics) that apply internationally may not necessarily apply in the United States.
U.S. Availability Is Not the Same as U.S. Legality
Even if a platform is accessible from the United States, it may not be licensed or authorized to operate there: online crypto casino is licensed in offshore jurisdictions, and many platforms, which would otherwise be legal in the United States, have terms of service that specifically restrict American users.
However, just because a betting site is available does not necessarily mean it is legal or regulated. Players should check that a site is licensed in their jurisdiction, and carefully read its terms and conditions and player eligibility terms in the operator’s legal text.
No KYC Crypto Casino: Privacy Benefit or Compliance Risk?
No KYC crypto casinos allow players to create accounts and make deposits without verification during the signup process, but additional verification may be required at a later point. Other operators may require identity documents for AML, fraud prevention, or licensing requirements, typically when users make large withdrawals or have unusual account activity.
While onboarding may be more private since it would reduce KYC information, it may be unclear if players were only KYC’d upon their intention to withdraw. A no-KYC policy is only as credible as its documentation.
How We Verify No-KYC Claims
As a rule, the use of terms such as anonymous crypto casino or “no KYC” is not based on marketing material, but is verified through the Terms and Conditions, AML policy, withdrawal policies, and other publicly available information.
However, if published policies allow collecting identity checks under specific circumstances, the operator cannot be classified as providing unconditional no-KYC account access.
No KYC Does Not Always Mean No Verification
Thus, “no KYC” usually means no verification is required when registering, although it is common for operators to ask for identity documents before a withdrawal, during a risk review, or to comply with local regulations.
So this report’s “no KYC crypto casino” status may simply refer to its current onboarding practices, not a guarantee that users will never be asked to verify.

The primary value of a no-deposit crypto casino bonus is that it allows a player to try out a new site at no cost. However, no deposit crypto bonuses should not be treated as free money, as most are attached to terms such as wagering requirements, withdrawal limits, game exclusions, or a limited time period for withdrawals. The value of a promotion may depend on the full disclosure and applicability of its terms, rather than only their maximum potential value. For example, a small bonus with simple conditions may be more desirable than a large bonus with withdrawal restrictions.

For this reason, crypto casino bonus mechanisms are evaluated in terms of the conditions listed on the bonus page. These include, but are not limited to, bonus terms, wagering conditions, eligible games, expiration period, and cash-out limits attached to a particular promotion.

Large promotions can be desirable, but may come with restrictions such as not being able to withdraw winnings, a maximum withdrawal limit that may be lower than the size of the bonus, high wagering requirements, banned games, or identity verification requirements.
For that reason, this report will first check whether the bonuses are transparent before evaluating the promotion. Transparent withdrawal conditions, reasonable wagering requirements, and the presence of terms are a good basis for that.
Crypto Casino Games: What Players Actually Play
Crypto casino games include customary casino games as well as games native to blockchain technology designed to be played using cryptocurrency. Online casinos comprise mostly slots, but crypto casinos popularized fast-paced, in-house games that allow outcomes to be determined instantly and are easy to understand, play, and allow users to bet using a crypto wallet.
In addition to games licensed from third-party game developers, many crypto casinos offer in-house games that use cryptographic verification to allow players to verify game outcomes without relying on third-party game certification services.
Slots, Crash Games, Dice, Plinko, and Live Dealer

It has also been joined by other crypto-native operators that offer crypto crash games, crypto dice, Plinko, limbo, and other self-developed games built for high-frequency play and the blockchain audience.
Other common games include table games, such as crypto roulette, crypto blackjack or crypto poker, and these games are either RNG games or live dealer games streamed from a professional studio. Fairness and verification of the game may differ depending on the format.
What “Provably Fair” Means — and Where It Falls Short
In a provably fair casino, the outcome of the game for a player’s bet may be verified as not being changed after the player’s bet is placed, using cryptography. This model is commonly used for the larger games in the house, including dice, crash, Plinko, and mines, among others, which all provide verifiable outcomes.
Provably fair verification is not applicable to all types of casino games, and many third-party slots use certified random number generators instead of player-verifiable cryptography. Similarly, games that use mechanical cards or roulette wheels, such as live dealer games, cannot be verified that way.
In this sense, “provably fair” should be understood in terms of this specific game feature, not the platform in general.
Payments and Withdrawals: The Real Test of a Crypto Casino
While crypto casino payments may be settled on the blockchain relatively quickly, the payout time is also affected by the operator’s internal withdrawal approval process (verification if needed, how many steps are involved, etc.). It is most noticeable when withdrawing funds.

Most major operators now accept crypto deposits and withdrawals in Bitcoin, Ethereum, USDT, and several other altcoins. New operators may offer a modern UI, support for a wider array of crypto betting, sports, and esports betting options to differentiate themselves from existing platforms. However, they may not have proven themselves in terms of reliability and payouts.
Since the newer platforms are so young, this research is focused on the licensing and ownership structure, payment structure, and policies rather than marketing claims or social media.
How to Evaluate a New Operator With Limited Reputation History
When reviewing a new online crypto casino, important independently verifiable factors such as licensing, company information, security, payment networks, KYC requirements, and withdrawal and bonus rules should be considered and weighed carefully.
Low player feedback and short operating history could indicate risk, but certainly aren’t definitive. Platforms that have been around for a shorter time also need special attention. Conclusions should be based on evidence and facts, and not solely on what the platform wants you to believe.
Crypto Casino Risk Rating
Conceptually, it uses a qualitative risk model, prioritizing on-chain transparency over the casino’s reputation. The methodology considers only documents and information made public at the start and the end of the review period for each individual point.
This includes licensing disclosures, ownership disclosures, withdrawal policies, KYC documentation, payment transparency, and responsible gambling policy.

As a point of clarification, a higher score is not necessarily always worse or a lower score is not necessarily always better: it is simply a comparable measure of a risk factor.

What We Do Not Recommend
Moreover, this crypto casino research does not recommend any operators without minimum transparency information, including licensing, ownership, payment policies, or any other information necessary to offer a reasonable assessment.
Transparency should be publicly verifiable. These elements are key to responsible crypto casino licensing and regulation.

Alternatively, if a site has a poor reputation for paying out or changing their withdrawal requirements, or requiring an extra level of verification that was not stated in the terms, it should be viewed as a red flag. Transparency is better than marketing.

results.title: Not all gaming consoles are worth the splurge — these ones are
results.author: Nishka Dhawan
results.content:
As a girl who’s gamed all her life — and whose first console was the PlayStation Portable (sorry, Game Boy lovers) — I’ve tried my fair share of gaming consoles.
Everything from the Xbox Kinect to the Wii has held a place in my home, along with more recent options like the Xbox Series X and Nintendo Switch 2.
After spending way too many hours playing games like “Baldur’s Gate 3,” “Pokémon Pokopia,” all the “Zelda” installments (and much, much more), it’s safe to say I know what makes a good gaming console.
From considering playable titles to space and essential hardware, I’ve found the best gaming consoles and listed them right below. You might already own some of these, but here’s hoping that I convince you to try something new.
Best gaming consoles
Best Microsoft Console: Xbox Series X
Pros:
- True 4K gaming with up to 120 FPS
- 1TB of storage
- Works with physical game discs and Blu-rays
- Strong performance for heavier games
- Durable console and controllers
- Access to Game Pass
- Quick Resume makes it easy to jump back into games
- Better fit than Series S if you want physical copies
Cons:
- Bulky design
- Heavier than some other consoles
- More expensive than the Series S
- Takes up more space than a handheld or slim console
- Some games can still have bugs or performance issues
I’ve owned my Xbox Series X for almost six years now, which seems crazy to me, and there’s nothing I’d change about it — apart from the bugs in some of the games I play.
I’ve also tried the Series S, which does offer a space-saving design, but I personally love owning physical copies of games and loading them into my Xbox. In fact, the Xbox also works as a DVD player, so you can use it to play any old Blu-rays you have.
Mine has 1TB of storage and streams in 4K, while the Series S can only do 1440p, and games look almost lifelike on my widescreen TV. My console seamlessly runs heavy-duty games like “Forza Horizon 6” or “Baldur’s Gate 3” with little to no issues. One of my favorite features is being able to save games. Even if you uninstall, once you’re ready to play again, you can pick up right where you started.
Refresh rates up to 120 frames per second also mean I can play first-person shooter games on the console, like “Halo,” without any lag. I use my Xbox with the included controllers, and the best part is that even though I’ve accidentally dropped them off my bed at least a dozen times, they function just fine and have no visual damage.
I also love the Xbox-exclusive games — yes, I’m going to say “Forza” again — that make the Xbox the gift that keeps on giving. I’m subscribed to Game Pass, which gives access to hundreds of games every month, including a ton of new titles, so you never get bored.
The Series X is a little bulky, weighing close to 10 pounds, and it’s a rectangular brick that can’t easily be missed. But for the performance, ease of use and clear durability, it’s well worth its price.
Storage: 1TB SSD | Resolution: True 4K gaming | Frame rate: Up to 120 FPS | Disc drive: 4K UHD Blu-ray drive | Weight: 9.8 pounds | Dimensions: 5.9 inches. x 5.9 inches. x 11.9 inches.
Best Sony console: PlayStation 5 (Disc Edition)
Pros:
- Strong exclusive games
- Easy to switch between streaming apps and games
- Ultra HD Blu-ray disc drive
- Up to 4K gaming and 120 FPS
- Easier to clean than some older consoles
- Quieter performance, according to our tester
Cons:
- PS5 design can be awkward to fit in some media centers.
- More expensive than the digital edition.
- Some of the best features, like 4K/120Hz gameplay, depend on having a compatible TV
While I don’t own the PlayStation 5, I have gamed on one, and our commerce partnerships manager, Frank Massaro, owns and loves it.
New York Post Review: “My PlayStation 5 is the hero of our media center. The seamless switch from watching Netflix to hopping into the latest gaming title (I’m currently playing “Star Wars Bad Company”) means that the PS5 is constantly being used during those essential unwind periods.
“The ability to easily clean the console was an unforeseen perk. I have had many gaming consoles start to sound like airplanes taking off due to wear and tear and dust intake. Sony has made the PS5 easily accessible for those routine cleanings, and my console is as quiet as a mouse.
“Sony has invested heavily into its first-party IPs. With titles like “God of War,” “Ratchet & Clank,” “Astro Bot,” Insomniac’s “Spider-Man” and the upcoming ‘Wolverine,’ the best games are simply available on PlayStation.
“Having a PlayStation and a PlayStation Plus membership means you get a steady monthly cadence of free games, so you will never have a shortage of options for entertainment.”
Storage: 1TB custom SSD | Resolution: 4K gaming | Frame rate: Up to 120 FPS with 120Hz output | Disc drive: Ultra HD Blu-ray disc drive | Weight: 6.8 pounds | Dimensions: 14.1 inches. x 3.8 in. x 8.5 inches.
Best 2-1- consoleNintendo Switch 2
Pros:
- Works as both a handheld console and traditional TV console
- Supports up to 4K output when docked
- Larger 7.9-inch display than the original Switch
- Joy-Con 2 controllers attach magnetically, which feels more streamlined
- Built-in microphone for GameChat
- Most Nintendo Switch games are compatible with Switch 2
Cons:
- LCD screen is not as vivid as the Nintendo Switch OLED
- Battery life can vary a lot depending on the game
- Some older Nintendo Switch games may not be supported or fully compatible
- 4K output requires a compatible TV and game
I got the original Nintendo Switch the second it launched, and since then, I’ve also owned the Nintendo Switch OLED and now, as of this February, the Nintendo Switch 2.
The reason the Switch 2 stands out for me is simple: Nintendo completely redesigned the way the Joy-Con controllers attach to the device, not just increasing their durability, so gaming on it a much more streamlined experience.
I love how the Switch has the ability to easily transform from a handheld device to a traditional console, which now supports 4K when docked. It also has a built-in mic for GameChat, which lets you speak to your friends no matter where they are while you game. The display is wider than before, though unlike the OLED, the screen here is LCD, so you miss out on the clarity when the device is in handheld mode.
That said, most older games are still compatible on the Switch 2, though some titles are Switch 2-specific, like “Pokémon Pokopia.”
Storage: 256GB UFS | Resolution: 4K gaming in TV mode; 1920 x 1080 handheld | Frame rate: Up to 120 FPS with 120Hz output; 4K capped at 60 FPS | Disc drive: None | Weight: 1.18 pounds with Joy-Con 2 controllers attached | Dimensions: 10.7 in. x 4.5 inches. x 0.55 inches.
Best Portable: Steam Deck
Pros:
- Portable design
- Large Steam library
- Strong screen quality
- Console-like controls
- Expandable storage
- Great for travel, commuting and couch gaming
Cons:
- Bulkier than some handheld consoles
- Battery life varies depending on the game
- Some PC titles may need tweaking before they run smoothly
- Works best if you already use Steam as your main gaming library
I had a chance to check out the Steam Deck while visiting my brother-in-law in India, and I was immediately impressed by the screen quality and portable design, plus the ability to play hundreds of games on the go.
After spending a few hours gaming on it, I asked my brother-in-law, Nishant, a lawyer by day and gamer by night, what he thought about the Steam Deck.
“As a working man, I was never able to get into console or PC gaming again since I spent most of my time either at work, in commute or on the couch watching TV with my better half,” he shared. “I couldn’t hog the TV or spend time in front of a PC after a day at work.
“Then I got the Steam Deck and NGL it changed my life. The Steam Deck gave me the ease of console gaming with the economics of PC gaming. I play during commute, I play while watching TV, I play on vacation and sometimes, I play at work.
“I have spent around 900 Hours in almost 3 years on my steam deck and have fully completed 38 titles. And I had a blast playing each and every one of them. I don’t know what fps I was getting, all I know is that I haven’t had this much fun gaming since I got the PS3 in school.
I find myself thinking this almost constantly: The steam deck made me fall in love with gaming again.”
Storage: 512GB or 1TB NVMe SSD | Resolution: 1280 x 800 HDR OLED | Frame rate: Up to 90 FPS with 90Hz refresh rate | Disc drive: None | Weight: 1.41 pounds | Dimensions: 11.7 in. x 4.6 in. x 1.9 in.
Add on gaming accessories
This article was written by Nishka Dhawan, Commerce Reporter for the New York Post. Nishka reports on the latest tech launches, innovations and trends to separate the best new products from the “AI slop.” Taking the latest technology for a spin, Nishka tests home appliances and tech products that actually improve your life, from vacuums to headphones to gaming gadgets and more – all while finding the best deals and lowest prices. Before joining The Post in 2026, her work appeared in Rolling Stone, ABC, NBC Select, Reviewed and Digital Trends.

results.title: Mario-a-Lago Kart, Anyone?
results.author: Emily Bressler, Kelley Greene
results.content:
This week, the White House removed a Tetris-inspired game called Build the Wall from its recently launched arcade website after the Tetris Company publicly warned that it takes copyright law “very seriously.”
Here are a few options the White House might consider to replace the game:
Super PAC-Man
Players direct a round creature with a constantly moving mouth through a maze as he munches on tiny coins. Meanwhile, the ghosts of financial lawsuits past pursue Super PAC-Man—but consuming excerpts from favorable Supreme Court rulings allows him to temporarily devour these ghosts, too. Once Super PAC-Man collects all the coins, he progresses, unsatiated, to the next level, where he sends out a single text and all the money starts flowing directly toward him.
Words With Enemies
Players form new, hateful attacks in this Scrabble-like multiplayer game using letters cut from public-school textbooks, removed museum displays, and maps depicting the former Lake Ontario. Highest-scoring insults include: SCUZZY, ZANY, and LOW-IQ JOKER. Extra points are awarded for letters placed on various Random Capitalization Squares.
Mario-a-Lago Kart
Up to four players race golf carts around a cartoonishly decorated beach club, crashing through boxes of classified documents to unlock power-ups including nuclear footballs and black markers for unlimited redactions. Between races, players can refuel at the gas pump, assuming they have collected the requisite 175,000 coins per gallon. The winner receives a golf trophy; second, third, and fourth place—as well as any observers or people simply standing nearby—get access to state secrets.
Grand Theft Crypto
This game is all in the timing: Players must market their own cryptocurrency, then wait until just the right moment to cash out, crashing the currency and tanking other players’ life savings.
The Oregon Data Center
Modern-day pioneers move into a covered wagon after an eminent-domain order for the construction of a data center displaces them from their hometown. Drinking water is scarce, noise pollution is earsplitting, and morale is low as players try to survive the perilous journey to one of the few remaining corners of protected parkland. Inevitably, all players die when artificial general intelligence bioengineers a new form of dysentery.
Goldeneye
In this first-person interior-design game, players gild every nook, cranny, and free patch of wall space in their virtual home office.
Coal Minecraft
No longer beholden to child-labor regulations, players ages 6 to 8 design their own pickaxes before descending 1,500 feet down a shaft to mine bituminous coal. Open-world play means that the only limit is kids’ imagination and black lung and tunnel collapse.
Super Smash the Kennedy Center
Players battle conservationists, historians, and patrons of the arts atop a revered memorial building, destroying it in the process. Downloadable content expands play to the Reflecting Pool, the National Mall, and the East Wing of the White House.
Candy Crush the American Dream
Players rearrange foods that were once safe to eat into matching groups to make them disappear as part of an FDA recall. But miss just one, and players will contract a parasitic infection that sends them to the hospital, where they will incur astronomical medical bills, which will prevent them from qualifying for a mortgage, which will force them to move back in with their parents.
President Evil
A zombie occupies the most powerful office in the world. At the conclusion of Level 2, President Evil might insist that the game isn’t over, but so long as it works as intended, someone else will finally get a turn to play.

If you're not yet subscribed to Tom's Hardware Premium, we've got you covered with this weekly roundup of everything we've posted throughout the week.
To kick the week off, our resident GPU guru and all-round inference extraordinaire Jeff Kampman undertook the laborious task of running Qwen 3.8 27B across several devices you might actually be able to afford. The model promises near-enough Frontier levels of performance, without the downsides that come alongside paying for an API-based subscription or tokenized billing.
What Jeff finds out after a dizzyingly large number of benchmarks across devices like an RTX 5090, Mac Mini, DGX Spark, and Strix Halo systems is that configuration matters just as much as the final, raw, tokens-per-second outputs that many clamor over on social media. Benchmarking AI models is still a fairly nascent subject, and the level of detail on offer here isn't something you'll find published anywhere else.
Andrew Freedman headed out to IFA last week, where we saw a slew of new announcements and devices from companies. But there's only one problem. They're all either super-light MacBook Neo competitors or Agentic AI PCs that may well cost more than a car. The original "golden" price point for many enthusiasts, around $1,000, looks a little lonely as a result.
The factors impacting the mid-range of regular old desktops and laptops have been adversely affected by the sheer scale of demand coming from the ongoing AI data center buildout. Meaning that if you're after a system with just enough RAM and storage to get by, prices can skyrocket fast. Andrew explores everything he saw at the show and ruminates on the current state of the systems market, which, for now, appears to be fractured.
Elsewhere in the industry, Ajinomoto, a company usually associated with food products based in Japan, is involved in making some of the most crucial materials in modern AI accelerators. We've taken a look at how the company's ABF substrates sit within the supply chain of the biggest chipmakers like Nvidia, Intel and AMD. But, as with many components in the AI boom, it's strained by more demand than anyone anticipated, which has led to an increase in prices of approximately 30%. We dive deep into the current state of the use of ABF substrates in the semiconductor industry and take a look at the supply chains underpinning it.
Also in the news, TSMC, Intel, and Samsung have all thrown their support behind ASML. The industry is collectively aiming to move towards a shift in High-NA EUV, particularly in the usage of 6×12-inch photomasks. With current standards set at 6×6-inch photomasks, a larger mask would eliminate the need for stitching, which weaves together multiple High-NA exposures, at the cost of efficiency.

results.title: Studio Behind Critically-Acclaimed PSVR Game Shuts Down After 12 Years
results.author: Ethan Gach
results.content:
PlayStation VR shipped in 2016. Two years later, Polyarc released Moss, a puzzle fantasy adventure featuring an adorable mouse named Quill. It ended up being nominated for a slew of awards and proved that virtual reality could be more than just a gimmick for creating new types of video game experiences. One sequel and a non-VR adaptation later, Polyarc is shutting down.
“After nearly 12 years riding the joyous rollercoaster of emotions that is making video games, our time together has come to an end,” the studio announced in a statement on LinkedIn. “As we wind down active development, we are saying our farewells to each other.”
It continued, “Working together over all of these years has been an honor. Bringing surprise and delight to those who played our games has been a privilege. Thank you to everyone at Polyarc, our work is now finished. Polyarc has been home to exceptional developers across all disciplines. If you are hiring, please see the link below.”
The VR market has not been kind to those who invested in it, including the ones like Polyarc that created genuinely great and worthwhile games that can’t be experienced anywhere else. Moss: Book II was released in 2022 for PS VR2. It successfully iterated on the combat and emotional beats of the first game, going on to win best VR game of the year at The Game Awards 2022.
But improvements to the technology haven’t expanded VR’s reach or the audience for games specializing in it. While companies like Valve continue to invest in new headset hardware, others like Meta and PlayStation have noticeably pulled back. Earlier this year, Polyarc released a version of both Moss games recreated for regular 2D TV displays, but much of the magic was lost along the way.
“Goodbye Polyarc, you (and Quill) will be remembered,” ex-PlayStation exec Shuhei Yoshida, who helped spearhead the company’s VR initiative, wrote on X. “We had great times together.”

results.author: Davidbombal, Davidb_Admin

Big thanks to @ThreatLocker for sponsoring my trip to Black Hat USA 2026 and also for sponsoring this video. To start your free trial with ThreatLocker please use the following link: https://www.threatlocker.com/davidbombal
You can write secure C code, follow accepted best practices and still end up with a vulnerable binary. The reason is simple: the CPU does not run your source code. It runs whatever the compiler produces.
David sits down with security researcher Chris Domas at Black Hat to examine how legal compiler optimizations can remove security protections, delete memory-clearing operations and introduce time-of-check to time-of-use vulnerabilities into code that appeared secure.
Chris explains the C abstract machine, why compilers are allowed to transform code so dramatically and how register pressure, structure layout and even data size can affect whether a binary is vulnerable. In one striking example, 17 or 33 bytes can be safe while nearby sizes produce vulnerable code. They also discuss whether Rust solves the problem, why switching between GCC and Clang is not the answer and how AI helped analyse 500 million lines of open-source code to identify 300 potentially dangerous patterns.
Most importantly, Chris explains what developers can do now, including enabling compiler warnings, using sanitizers, analysing optimized builds and testing the exact binary that will be shipped.

Security researcher Chris Domas explains how compiler optimizations can inadvertently introduce critical vulnerabilities into C code, even when developers follow established best practices for writing secure software.

### Key Points
- Compilers may remove security protections or memory-clearing operations during the optimization process, rendering seemingly secure source code vulnerable.
- Data structure layout, register pressure, and specific data sizes can unpredictably influence whether a compiled binary contains exploitable security flaws.
- AI-driven analysis of 500 million lines of open-source code successfully identified 300 potentially dangerous patterns caused by compiler transformations.
- Developers are advised to enable compiler warnings, utilize sanitizers, and perform rigorous testing on the final optimized binaries intended for production.
- Switching between common compilers like GCC and Clang does not inherently resolve these optimization-related security risks.

### Why it Matters
These findings highlight a significant disconnect between secure source code and the final executable binary produced by modern compilers. Understanding these risks is essential for developers to prevent silent security regressions that occur during the build process.

results.title: The mathematicians rebel against AI
results.author: Tyler Cowen
results.content:
Here is the statement, signed by Terry Tao among many other math notables, most of you probably have read it by now. I do not accept the most cynical interpretations of this proclamation. Some of you for instance may recall that I made and indeed stressed a similar point in the last chapter of my recent “generative book” on marginalism. In some near future, perhaps fewer economists will carry around marginalist insights and modes of thought in their heads, since you can just get the right answer by pressing the proverbial button on the AI.
I find this future disturbing, and not altogether pleasant for me personally, given how much personal status I have wrapped up in particular modes of economic thought. Yet I also know the Bastiat distinction between the seen and the unseen, and I expect the benefits to economic science from AI will be enormous, even if current practitioners cannot foresee most of those benefits today.
I do very much differ with at least one part of the mathematicians’ proclamation. They write: “…whether these changes ultimately benefit the field or have a destructive effect will in large part be determined by the decisions of the humans in control of this new technology.” There is no actual argument for that proposition, and I would sooner expect that the main “action variable” is how well the mathematicians adapt to the new reality. For instance there is nothing stopping the mathematics community from awarding status, pay, and promotions to people who “fill in the important blanks in math understanding,” even if an AI already has proven or disproven the underlying theorems. If that kind of work is so important, we still can do it and reward it professionally. In the meantime, I expect the funding for mathematics, and the interest in the topic, to rise considerably, at least in the medium term. All of a sudden, math matters much more than it used to, all the more so if P vs. NP happens to go the wrong way, or if the distribution of the primes turns out to be a little too predictable.
The mathematicians may not in every way enjoy being the subordinates or handmaidens of the AIs, but that is a change in status they simply will have to get used to, just as I realize AIs someday will end up as better column and blog writers than I am. I do not look to the companies — which I fully expect to “act like companies” — to somehow manage, moderate, or assuage that pending trend. It really is up to me to parlay my current intellectual portfolio into new, more AI-compatible intellectual and yes also marketing approaches. I’ve been given plenty of “legs up” along the way already, as is true for the Fields Medal winners as well, and it is up to me to figure out how to contribute in the future.
Might someone not invent/discover/prompt a way to use AIs to produce, articulate, and teach “more mathematical understanding” along the way? I get that solving famous dramatic math problems is the current commercial priority of the major AI companies. But as the AI space grows, these other paths hardly seem unlikely to me, and in fact the human mathematicians are the ones who can do the most to lead the way along those dimensions.
In this regard the current manifestation of complaints seems oddly early. “I didn’t like the first week or two of your intellectual revolution” is an accurate, and perhaps better reframed way of putting it. At which point perhaps a bit of patience is needed before anything else? These days, we all have more mathematical resources at our disposal, and so a bit of celebration is in order as well.

Reverse engineering notes, deobfuscated source, IOCs, and YARA rules for the Tourmaline ClickFix Python RAT, covering its DNS tunnel and blockchain dead-drop C2.
I recently stumbled upon a piece of cleverly designed malware that calls itself "Torumaline".
This README is very kindly written by Claude as I was super busy with exams at the time of this repository's inception.
Exploiting and decrypting this malware took a huge chunk of my time from math prep!
Read the blogpost!
FOR EDUCATIONAL AND RESEARCH PURPOSES ONLY
All samples are provided for malware analysis and defensive research. Do not execute outside a sandboxed, air-gapped environment.
Tourmaline (Tourmaline.exe) is a sophisticated, multi-stage Windows infostealer/backdoor distributed via a ClickFix campaign - a fake Cloudflare "Verify you are human" browser popup that tricks users into manually running a malicious command or installer.
The binary is a custom-built Inno Setup 6.7.0 (Revision 2, 64-bit offsets) installer that bundles a full Python 3.11 runtime and two stages of obfuscated Python payload. It establishes a persistent backdoor with:

├── LICENSE                    # Research use license
├── .gitignore
│
├── src/                       # Extracted & deobfuscated source code
│   ├── stage1_loader.py       # Stage 1: Original obfuscated XOR time-lock loader (main.py)
│   ├── stage2_backdoor.py     # Stage 2: Deobfuscated core backdoor (from QGBdu.dxf)
│   └── decrypt_payload.py     # Utility: O(1) payload key recovery & decryption
│
├── iocs/                      # Indicators of Compromise
│   ├── indicators.json        # Structured IOC data (IPs, hashes, domains, registry)
│   ├── indicators.csv         # Flat CSV for SIEM import
│   └── rules.yar              # YARA detection rules
│
└── samples/                   # Malware samples (password-protected)
    ├── README.md              # Sample archive instructions
    ├── Tourmaline_sample.zip  # Password: infected - contains Tourmaline.exe
    └── QGBdu.dxf             # Raw encrypted Stage 2 payload blob
The malware is distributed via ClickFix - a social engineering technique where a compromised or attacker-controlled website overlays a fake Cloudflare CAPTCHA or browser verification page. The overlay instructs the victim to:
Win+R
The pasted command downloads and silently executes Tourmaline.exe. The installer runs /VERYSILENT /SUPPRESSMSGBOXES /NORESTART.
Note: Stock innoextract 1.9 cannot extract this binary — it only supports Revision 1. Revision 2 uses 64-bit offsets and requires custom parsing (see src/decrypt_payload.py).
Tourmaline.exe
│
├─ Inno Setup installer runs silently
│   ├─ Extracts Python 3.11 runtime to %APPDATA%\Tourmaline\
│   ├─ Extracts main.py (Stage 1 loader)
│   ├─ Extracts QGBdu.dxf (encrypted Stage 2 blob)
│   ├─ Kills any existing pythonw.exe instances
│   └─ Registers persistence (Task Scheduler / registry)
│       └─ Name: "TourmalineUpdate" / "Hardware monitoring service"
│
├─ Stage 1: main.py (XOR Time-Lock Loader)
│   ├─ Counts _n from 99,999,999 → 0 (anti-sandbox delay ~hours on slow VMs)
│   ├─ At each _n, constructs 33-byte XOR key: struct.pack('>I', _n) + hardcoded_suffix
│   ├─ Tests key against known plaintext header of QGBdu.dxf
│   └─ On match: decrypts QGBdu.dxf entirely and exec()s the result
│       └─ O(1) bypass: known-plaintext attack on first 4 bytes (see below)
│
└─ Stage 2: QGBdu.dxf → Python backdoor
    ├─ Reads MachineGuid from HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Cryptography
    ├─ Derives mutex Global\Tourmaline_<hash>
    ├─ Resolves C2 IP via Ethereum dead-drop (Sepolia testnet)
    ├─ Establishes DNS tunnel to C2
    └─ Poll-execute loop: fetches tasks, exec()s Python, returns output
The loader (main.py) uses a countdown from 99,999,999 to find the XOR decryption key. On a real machine this completes in seconds (because _n starts high and the true value is near 14,511,188). In a sandbox with a short time limit, the loop never completes.
Key structure:
full_key = struct.pack('>I', _n) + bytes.fromhex('2b0cffe07b06ac25793b3f00cfaa2dd5881c2d6378165247539dbbdaeb')
Since we know the first 16 bytes of the plaintext (g1 = lambda l6, ), we can recover _n instantly via known-plaintext XOR attack:
key_prefix = bytes(ciphertext[i] ^ known_plaintext[i] for i in range(4))
# Result: key_prefix = 00dd6c54 → _n = 14,511,188
Use src/decrypt_payload.py to reproduce this.
The malware calls an Ethereum smart contract on the Sepolia testnet to retrieve the active C2 IP address. This means the attacker can change the C2 IP at any time by updating the contract — traditional IP blocklist-based C2 disruption is ineffective.
Contract : 0x2d7a04cca0c34005f58393f30ac725e25f19e5f5
Selector : 0xeb9fd6fe
Network  : Ethereum Sepolia (chainId 11155111)
RPC      : https://ethereum-sepolia-rpc.publicnode.com
Result   : ChaCha20-encrypted blob containing current C2 IP
The returned data is decrypted with the hardcoded ChaCha20 key to reveal the live C2 address. At time of analysis, this resolved to 158.94.211.185 (verified via live RPC call).
All C2 traffic is sent as raw UDP DNS queries directly to the C2 IP on port 53. Queries are structured as <encoded_data>.microsoft.com, bypassing DNS-based filtering and appearing as legitimate Windows telemetry.
socket.getaddrinfo or any DNS library
